01

Problem & Scope

A shopping collection is useful only when it can be read again.

A draft becomes a real record

Choose sneakers, a tee, a hoodie or a backpack. Build an order locally, then save it through an authenticated API. Read it again, rename it, change its items, or delete it.

One flow, two data models

PostgreSQL stores the parent order and its related item rows. MongoDB stores one order document with embedded items. The engine selector chooses one destination—not both.

Small, intentional scope. Four catalog products, quantity 1–9, anonymous demo sessions, and genuine order/item CRUD. No payments, inventory, shipping, cross-engine synchronization or distributed transaction.

Local draft ≠ saved orderServer-owned pricesOwner-scoped recordsSeparate engines

Architecture Concepts

Six boundaries from a local draft to a verified saved order.

01 · React state

Draft state

Draft products and estimates live in page memory. A database commit saves the record; a fresh read confirms the result.

React · State as a Snapshot ↗ 02 · Identity + ownership

Identity and ownership

Anonymous sign-in creates an identity. The API verifies its token and checks ownership before accessing an order.

Supabase · Anonymous Sign-Ins ↗ 03 · Trusted API boundary

Trusted validation

Validate known products, labels and quantities server-side. Trusted backend catalog values—not browser prices—determine integer-cent totals.

OWASP · Input Validation Cheat Sheet ↗ 04 · Relational integrity

Relational integrity

Foreign keys connect orders, items and immutable products. Owner-checking SQL transactions keep related changes together.

PostgreSQL · Transactions ↗ 05 · Embedded aggregate

Embedded orders

Embedded items need no joins. Item edits are atomic; order creation and deletion also transact against the owner quota.

MongoDB · Atomicity and Transactions ↗ 06 · Verified outcomes

Verified read-back

Validate responses, then read again before showing success. Ignore stale replies and refresh before repeating an uncertain write.

MDN · Using the Fetch API ↗
03

System Architecture

Follow the trust boundary. Compare the two consistency boundaries.

One authenticated API chooses one database per request. Follow the numbered path from a memory-only draft to a fresh verified read. The two storage models are alternatives—not replicas. This is a design map, not live telemetry.

Read the persistence path and its limits

1 · Browser state and session state are independent

The bundled catalog permits browsing before connection. React draft items and estimates live only in page memory; reloading discards them. Start demo session explicitly requests anonymous Auth. Browser storage can recover that session on reload, but cannot recover the draft. The anonymous signed-in user has the authenticated role, unlike the unauthenticated anon project role. Signing out or clearing storage loses anonymous access, not the saved records themselves.

2 · Auth verifies identity; the API establishes authority

The shipped UI sends bearer-authenticated requests to one Edge Function. It calls GET /auth/v1/user to validate the access token rather than merely decoding a JWT, derives the owner from the verified user, and ignores submitted owner identities. It validates known product IDs, label length of 1–80 Unicode code points and integer quantities 1–9. Amounts come from the selected trusted backend path, not universally from the Edge controller: the SQL RPC computes totals from immutable product joins; MongoDB server catalog snapshots feed normalization and cents totals. The internal router selects exactly one engine; neither catalog nor router is a separate microservice.

3 · SQL: relationships plus an owner-checking transaction

The SQL adapter forwards the caller JWT and public project key to ss_orders_api. This SECURITY DEFINER RPC derives auth.uid(), revalidates input and performs explicit owner checks for each operation. RLS is defense in depth; direct table grants are revoked. RLS alone is not the executed definer’s ownership guard, and the RPC also protects direct authenticated calls outside this UI.

ss_private.orders is the parent of ss_private.order_items. Foreign keys link order_id to the parent and product_id to immutable products. SQL item rows contain quantity, not name or price snapshots: reads join product names and unit_price_cents from the catalog. The RPC’s multi-row changes are transactional; cascade delete removes child rows. See PostgreSQL’s foreign-key tutorial ↗ for the relationship boundary.

4 · MongoDB: one aggregate, with a deliberate quota exception

An owner-filtered findOne reads a full order; the owner-filtered list needs no joins. At most four embedded items hold productId, name, unitPriceCents and quantity. Item edits are single-document atomic. Create and delete instead use a two-document transaction: the order and ss_owner_caps count commit together to enforce ten orders per owner. The driver’s withTransaction helper can retry eligible transaction errors; its server-side retryWrites setting can also retry eligible writes. Neither is a browser retry of an HTTP write. MongoDB explains when to embed related data ↗ and driver transaction behavior ↗.

5 · Verify the outcome; preserve uncertainty honestly

Database persistence happens at commit; read-back confirms subsequent observable committed state. It is confirmation, not the commit itself. JSON returns through the API. The client validates the HTTP envelope, engine, identifiers, quantities and cents totals, then performs a fresh record or list read before verified rendering; deletion is checked against the new list. Failed saves retain the draft. Switching engines cancels in-flight work and discards stale replies. Cancellation does not undo a committed write. There are no automatic browser HTTP write retries. A timeout may conceal a committed write: refresh before repeating an uncertain action. Rejected, malformed or unavailable responses remain errors, never synthetic saved orders.

The selector reads and writes only the selected engine. There is no cross-engine synchronization, dual write, shared transaction or distributed transaction across SQL and MongoDB. Separate records and different consistency boundaries are the point of this comparison.

Full implementation specification · suggested build prompt
StyleStore Saved Orders specification
Build a standalone StyleStore Saved Orders showcase.

1. Deliver a seven-section HTML shell with an isolated React storefront.
   Preserve source-derived header, adaptive product card, order summary,
   local theme packages, native prompt disclosures and copy controls.
   Do not modify the source portfolio or load cloud theme preferences.

2. Bundle four illustrated products: Retro Sneakers (8500 USD cents),
   Classic Tee (2800), Everyday Hoodie (6400), City Backpack (5200).
   Local drafts are page-memory estimates, never database records.
   Limit each product to one line with integer quantity 1–9.

3. Use Supabase JS anonymous Auth only after Start demo session.
   Recover the dedicated saved-orders-auth session after reload.
   Public config.js contains supabaseUrl, publishableKey and the
   saved-orders function name. Never include privileged credentials.
   Explain anonymous access loss before local sign-out.

4. Expose /catalog, /orders, /orders/:id, /orders/:id/items and
   /orders/:id/items/:itemId beneath one verified Edge Function.
   Use GET/POST/PATCH/DELETE as applicable with ?engine=sql|mongo.
   Validate the bearer token, derive owner identity server-side,
   validate labels of 1–80 characters and known product IDs, and
   calculate integer-cent totals from a trusted server catalog.

5. Implement PostgreSQL orders and order_items with foreign keys,
   owner policies and transactional RPC mutations. Implement MongoDB
   order documents with embedded items and atomic owner-filtered
   item changes. Create/delete also maintain an owner cap document
   transactionally; enforce ten saved orders per owner per engine.
   The selector chooses one engine per request. No syncing,
   dual writes or distributed transaction may be implied.

6. Provide draft building, order save/list/read/rename/delete and
   persisted item add/update/remove. Verify a write with a new read.
   Validate returned IDs, engine, item values and computed totals.
   Retain drafts on failure; never fabricate successful responses.
   Cancel superseded work, reject stale replies and never retry writes
   automatically. After an ambiguous write, refresh before repeating.

7. Label idle, unconfigured, unavailable, busy and verified outcomes.
   Keep tokens out of logs and optional JSON disclosures. Maintain
   visible focus, native labels and responsive card/summary stacking.
   Draw one accessible, uniformly scaling architecture SVG with the
   same viewBox and geometry at every viewport; no mobile replacement.

8. Write tests first and actually run the production build and browser.
   Check CRUD, ownership, limits, races, prompt clipboard, theme modes
   and 1920/1000/390/320px layouts. Distinguish unit fixtures from real
   database observations. Deliver only approved frontend/backend,
   configuration and tests; report unavailable dependencies honestly.
   Exclude payments, inventory, shipping, publication and unrelated
   account changes. Never include private conversations or secrets.

Audit

A design and code review contract—not completed runtime results.

Save contract · explanatory API excerpt
POST /orders?engine=sql|mongo
Authorization: Bearer <own session>
{ label, items: [{ productId, quantity }] }

API verifies identity → derives owner
Server catalog → price + totalCents
SQL: orders ← FK ← order_items
MongoDB: order { items: [...] }

Read back before verified success
Failure ≠ a saved order
No automatic write retries

Identity · derived, not supplied

The API derives ownership from verified Auth; a client-supplied owner is never authoritative.

Prices · server catalog

Requests contain product IDs and quantities, not trusted browser prices or totals.

Atomicity · engine-specific

SQL transactions join related rows; MongoDB updates one embedded order document.

Outcomes · read before success

Validate the returned record and read it again; failures never become synthetic saved orders.

06

Working System

Choose your essentials. Save an order. Read it again.

Build a local draft, then start a demo session to save an actual order. Use the engine selector to compare separate SQL and MongoDB records. A missing configuration or failed API stays unavailable—never a sample success.

The storefront requires JavaScript. No session has been started and no orders have been saved.

Draft → saved record

A draft is local; Save order writes through the API and verifies a new read.

Two independent engines

The selector chooses SQL or MongoDB; it never copies orders between them.

Your anonymous session

Reload keeps access when storage is available; sign-out loses anonymous access.

07

Verification

A short walkthrough to try against a configured backend.

  1. Save a collection. Start a session, add a few products, label the draft and save. Compare its verified server total with your selected quantities.
  2. Read and change it. Refresh or reload, open the saved order, rename it, change a quantity and remove an item. Read it again after each change.
  3. Try the other model. Switch engines and create a separate order. The original belongs only to the engine in which it was saved.
  4. Test limits and failure. Reach quantity 9, try an empty label, and retry a failed read. A failed save must not erase the local draft or claim success.
  5. Delete intentionally. Delete a saved order and confirm that a new list read no longer includes it. Sign-out is different: it loses access without deleting records.
  6. Use keyboard and mobile. Tab through themes, prompts and storefront controls. Copy a complete prompt, use both appearance modes, and inspect the same proportionally scaled map on a phone.

The UI stays familiar while the storage model changes. Relationships and embedded aggregates solve the same small problem with different consistency boundaries.
